doc.title: Lanny Morgan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Long drives, hotel day sheets and bad roads
summary: He explains driving through snow to one-nighters and the unfinished interstates.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: I didn’t quite follow — the day sheet?
Well the day sheet begins usually at 6 or 7:00 in the morning. In other words that’s that day.
Are you talking about a hotel?

It’s like this hotel ends, and they don’t want you to leave until eleven or noon maybe. But their sheet for new people checking in begins at probably seven or eight o’clock in the morning, if they have any rooms available then. So we would try and catch that and get a good day’s sleep and then leave after the job and drive all the way back to New York which was difficult.
You mean you drove to Chicago for a one-nighter?
Boy, I thought the rock & roll business was something.
No we did that quite a few times. We played Chicago and places like that.
And probably the thruway system, the roads were a long way from where they are now.

The thruways and the turnpikes were finished, but the interstates were not. And of course although we got reimbursed for tolls, it took time to stop and go through the toll booths all the time. And when you’re on a roll, you know I couldn’t drink during that period. I had to stay sober. Because driving through a blizzard with these guys— but you just get on a roll and you want to go. It’s kind of hypnotic, and I really shouldn’t have done that. But we would try these new interstates and they were a drag because you’d take an interstate for a hundred miles and you’d think oh this is wonderful, and they were brand new roads and so forth. And then it would say “END.” End of interstate. Merge into one lane. So you’d come into one lane and then it would take you probably an hour and a half to get back to a decent road. Because the interstates, if you notice on a map sometimes, go way far off of the freeways or the thruways. So that part of it was a drag, and there were some places like Cincinnati that it was almost impossible to get to. There were no decent roads. There were like a lot of two lane highways, back woods gas stations where you were almost afraid to stop sometimes, we had a couple of carloads of kids follow us into a gas station in West Virginia once and they had chains. You know they were going to get us good. Fortunately our car was newer and we got out of there fast. But there was a lot of that really. It was not completely safe to be traveling, even with six guys in the car.
